sections.h2: Where does a deed get recorded in Bernalillo County?
sections.html:
Deeds, mortgages, liens, judgments and plats are recorded by the Recording and Filing department of the Bernalillo County Clerk, at Alvarado Square, 415 Silver Ave SW in Albuquerque. The office phone is 505-468-1290 and the email is clerk@bernco.gov.

Bernalillo County covers 1,160 square miles and is New Mexico's most populous county, with more than 676,000 residents according to a county news release. Its government serves people in Albuquerque, Los Ranchos and Tijeras, and about 106,000 residents live in unincorporated areas. Every one of those parcels is recorded at this single office, since the county clerk keeps the land records for the county.

The clerk's Recording and Filing page lists hours of Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., with a lunch closure from noon to 1:15 p.m. The public access area, where you can search records yourself for free, runs 8 a.m. to 4:45 p.m.

sections.h2: What does the clerk require before it will record a deed?
sections.html:
The clerk needs the original document, signed and notarized, with the notary's stamp or seal and the full legal description of the property. A court document must be a certified copy bearing the court's stamp or seal.

The checklist from the clerk's page is short:

  • The original document, not a photocopy.
  • Signature and notarization, with the notary's seal and expiration date if there is one.
  • The full legal description of the Bernalillo County property.
  • The $25 recording fee, paid to BERNALILLO COUNTY.
  • A stamped, self-addressed envelope if you file by mail.

The office says it cannot give legal advice. Staff will not supply a form, tell you how to fill one out or confirm that you picked the right one, so the deed should be drafted by a title company, attorney or escrow officer before it arrives.

Recording makes the document part of the public record, which means anyone can read it. The clerk redacts parts of taxpayer ID numbers, financial account numbers, driver's license numbers, Social Security numbers and dates of birth, leaving the last four digits or the year.

sections.h2: What are the Bernalillo County recording fees?
sections.html:
Recording costs $25 per document for up to 10 entries, and a further $25 for each additional group of 10 or fewer. The county takes all payment methods except American Express.

ServiceFee
Record a document (up to 10 entries)$25
Each additional group of 10 entries or fewer$25
Copy, not certified$1 per page
Certified copy$2 per document, plus $1 per page
Electronic copy, emailed$1 per page
Faxed copy$2 plus the copy fee
Plat copy, 8.5 by 11 or 11 by 17 inches$1 per page

The fee schedule on the clerk's site is a list of recording and copy charges. It has no line for a transfer tax, so the clerk's side of a deed transfer is the $25 recording fee and any copies you order. Title, escrow and attorney charges are separate.

sections.h2: Can a deed be recorded electronically or by mail?
sections.html:
Yes to both. You can file in person with cash, card or check, mail the original to the clerk, or have a third-party vendor submit it electronically.

The mailing address is Bernalillo County Clerk's Office, Attn: Recording and Filing, P.O. Box 542, Albuquerque, NM 87103-0542. The clerk lists five electronic recording vendors: Kuvera Enterprise Solutions, Affiliated Computer Services, CSC eRecording Solutions, USA Digital Solutions and Simplifile. The page states that eRecording is not meant for individual use and that the list is not an endorsement. In practice, a title or escrow company usually handles that step.

Parking is free at 5th and Silver, with metered street parking nearby, per the clerk's FAQ.

sections.h2: What else must be filed with the County Assessor after a residential sale?
sections.html:
New Mexico law adds a second filing. Under section 7-38-12.1 NMSA 1978, a residential deed presented for recording must be followed by an affidavit filed with the county assessor within 30 days of the clerk's filing date.

The affidavit lists the names and mailing addresses of sellers and buyers, the legal description, the full consideration paid, any seller incentives, and the value of personal property included in the price. The statute says the information is for statistical and appraisal analysis and is kept as a confidential record by the assessor.

It is not required for every transfer. The exceptions in the statute include deeds for nonresidential property, conveyances under a court order, instruments that confirm or correct a recorded deed, transfers between spouses or between parent and child for nominal consideration, and instruments distributing a decedent's estate or trust. The Bernalillo County Assessor posts a Real Property Transfer Declaration Affidavit form, and the Assessor is at 505-222-3700.

sections.h2: How do I search Bernalillo County records and check for liens?
sections.html:
You can search the clerk's online index, which covers records from 1978 to the present, or use the free public access area at the office. Searches work by legal description, grantor and grantee names, or document number and date.

The clerk's FAQ is careful about limits. The office does not do full real estate searches or full lien checks, and says only a title company can run a full search. It also explains that a paid-off lien stays on the record until the lienholder files a Release of Lien. A seller who thinks an old contractor or judgment lien is long gone should ask for the recorded release, since a title company will otherwise raise the lien at closing.

Foreclosure and divorce records are not held by the clerk. They are kept by the Second Judicial District Court, which takes requests online.

sections.h2: What do sellers in Bernalillo County usually run into at the clerk's office?
sections.html:
The recurring problems involve whose name is on the deed. Three situations come up often, and the clerk's FAQ addresses each.

  • A surviving spouse who held the home in joint tenancy can bring a death certificate to the Assessor to update the name. If the property was not held that way, the clerk says probate court may be needed and recommends a lawyer.
  • An Assessor who asks for proof of ownership can be given a copy of a recorded deed or real estate contract obtained from the clerk.
  • A recorded lien that was paid but never released remains a cloud on title.

Each of those can slow a closing. A buyer paying cash and closing as-is still needs a clean chain of title, so these items are worth sorting out with a title company at the start of a sale.

The related Bernalillo County Treasurer page covers tax due at closing, and our Bernalillo County property tax guide covers the Assessor and the tax calendar.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to record a deed in Bernalillo County?
faqs.a: It costs $25 per document for up to 10 entries, and another $25 for each additional group of 10 or fewer. The clerk accepts all payment methods except American Express.

faqs.q: Does Bernalillo County charge a transfer tax on deeds?
faqs.a: The County Clerk's published fee schedule lists recording and copy fees only, with no transfer tax line. Closing costs from a title or escrow company are separate.

faqs.q: Do I need the original deed to record it?
faqs.a: Yes. The clerk needs the original, signed and notarized, with the full legal description. If you only have a record copy, a certified copy can be accepted, and the clerk will scan the original and return it.

faqs.q: Can I record a Bernalillo County deed by mail?
faqs.a: Yes. Mail the original, the $25 fee and a stamped return envelope to Bernalillo County Clerk's Office, Attn: Recording and Filing, P.O. Box 542, Albuquerque, NM 87103-0542.

faqs.q: What do I file with the Assessor after selling a house?
faqs.a: For residential property, an affidavit must be filed with the county assessor within 30 days of the date the deed was filed with the clerk, under section 7-38-12.1 NMSA 1978. Some transfers are exempt.

faqs.q: Where are foreclosure records for Bernalillo County kept?
faqs.a: They are kept by the Second Judicial District Court, not the County Clerk. The clerk's website links to the court's online request form.
